meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Victory belongs to the most persevering'?
meta.ogDescription: Credited to Napoleon everywhere, yet tied to no primary source. Earliest confirmed print: an 1888 school compilation. Here's the honest provenance.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Napoleon is credited with this line almost everywhere, and it is at least a genuinely old attribution — it appears in print by 1888. But no letter, speech, order, or maxim collection has been found that carries the wording, and the French form drifts between ‘plus persévérant’ and ‘plus opiniâtre.’ We can call it credibly attributed, not verified.

source.excerpt: Victory belongs to the most persevering.
trail: No Quote Investigator entry exists for this line, and it is absent from the Sourced section of Napoleon’s own Wikiquote page — it survives only as a topical attribution.
Wikiquote lists it on its Victory page, sourced only to a quotation compilation: “as quoted in Excellent Quotations for Home and School (1888) by Julia B. Hoitt, p. 51.”
We confirmed the line on p. 51 of the digitized 1888 book — but a school anthology quoting “Napoleon I.” is a second-hand attribution, not a primary source.

A tennis writer’s survey at Fiend at Court reaches the same conclusion: “no direct evidence that Napoleon actually said these precise words,” and the French form varies between persévérant and opiniâtre.
source.excerptNote: The oldest documented appearance we could confirm is in a school quotation book of 1888, where it sits under “Napoleon I.” in a “Guides to Conduct” section — with no citation to any work of Napoleon’s.

source.rightsNote: We could not tie this line to a specific work of Napoleon’s, so no copyright status is asserted for the quotation itself. The exact English wording is documented in the public-domain Excellent Quotations for Home and School (1888), but that anthology only quotes the line — it is not its source — and the underlying French phrasing has no identified original text or date.

author.name: Napoleon Bonaparte
author.heading: About the credited author
author.metaLine: 1769–1821 · French general, First Consul & Emperor of the French
author.bio: Napoleon Bonaparte rose from Corsican artillery officer to Emperor of the French, reshaping Europe through the Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars before his defeat at Waterloo and exile to Saint Helena. His restless, aphoristic style — captured in his correspondence, the Mémorial de Sainte-Hélène, and countless secondhand recollections — made him a magnet for punchy maxims, many of which cannot be traced to anything he actually wrote.

misattribution.heading: What's really going on
misattribution.intro: This is less a case of the wrong person than of a right-sounding line with no paper trail — and a wording that won’t hold still.

items.why: The line is credited to Napoleon across every major quote site, but none cites a letter, speech, or maxim. The earliest source anyone points to is a school quotation book of 1888 — decades after his death and with no reference to any work of his.

French sources split between « La victoire appartient au plus persévérant » and « … au plus opiniâtre » (most tenacious/stubborn). A stable Napoleon quote would not wobble between two different key adjectives, as Fiend at Court notes.

The ‘opiniâtre’ form is famous today because WWI aviator Roland Garros reportedly inscribed it on his aircraft propellers; it now adorns the Paris stadium named for him, which is where most people meet the line — not from any text of Napoleon’s.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuinely old and genuinely attributed to Napoleon — but attributed is as far as the evidence goes; no primary source confirms he ever wrote or said it, per Wikiquote.

context.heading: Why it stuck
lead: Napoleon is one of history’s great quotation magnets: a compact, commanding, aphoristic reputation that makes almost any crisp maxim about willpower or destiny sound plausible in his mouth. “Victory belongs to the most persevering” fits that mold perfectly, which is exactly why it needs scrutiny rather than trust.

The line’s modern fame owes less to Napoleon than to sport: as the motto associated with aviator Roland Garros and, through him, the French Open, it reaches millions each spring — cementing an attribution that no primary document supports.
context.pull: Old, ubiquitous, and unsourced — the three-word signature of a floating maxim.
